excess growth leading to infant obesity. In a Philippine cohort, larger weight increments from age 8–15 years increased risk of high
blood pressure in boys who were relatively thin at birth (Adair and Cole, 2003). However, higher childhood weight gain in the
absence of fetal growth restriction was not a risk factor in this population.
The physiological changes associated with a higher risk of hypertension following fetal undernutrition may include a reduced
number of nephrons. Such deﬁcits may not increase disease risk in individuals who remain small, but excess growth may challenge
the ability of the kidneys to effectively regulate blood pressure. Catch-up linear growth has not been consistently implicated as a risk
factor for later elevated blood pressure. In fact, continued poor linear growth, particularly in association with more rapid weight
gain, increases risk of later elevated blood pressure. Thus, it is important to consider both size at birth as well as post-natal growth
